Consistency.justification: The proposal closely follows the core idea: depth is patchified with a CNN, proprioception is embedded with an MLP, MAMBA is used for cross-modal fusion, PPO trains the controller, and domain randomization plus an obstacle curriculum support transfer. The hypotheses and evaluation metrics also reflect the stated goals of efficient, robust, vision-driven locomotion. However, the proposal adds substantial elements not central to the original idea, including differentiable MPC/iLQR, a learned contact residual, token-confidence supervision, hard safety shielding, and a fallback PD controller. These additions are potentially useful but make the claimed end-to-end framework less conceptually clean and are not adequately connected to the compact state-centric reward described in the idea. In fact, the reward itself is not explicitly formulated. There is also some tension between claiming an end-to-end policy and using planner targets, hard action replacement, and auxiliary gradients that allegedly do not directly update the policy head.

Clarity.justification: The proposal is well structured and provides concrete encoders, tokenization, gating equations, training settings, baselines, metrics, ablations, statistical procedures, and hardware targets. This makes the broad experimental plan easy to understand. Several important details remain ambiguous, however. It is not specified how spatial tokens are ordered for MAMBA scanning, whether temporal histories are included, or how dropping tokens affects positional information. The differentiable planner, contact residual, planner targets, policy residuals, and their gradient paths are described only at a high level. The statement that auxiliary losses backpropagate into perception and MAMBA but do not directly update the policy head does not fully clarify how shared-backbone changes interact with PPO. The safety-veto transition handling, advantage estimation, reward function, action space, control frequency, observation history, and exact architecture sizes are also missing. The use of a predicted confidence value as an input to the gating equation is potentially circular unless the computation order is defined.

Novelty.justification: Using a selective state-space backbone for multimodal fusion in vision-driven quadrupedal locomotion is a timely and reasonably original direction. The combination of MAMBA fusion, learned token budgeting, corruption-supervised token confidence, embedded deployment constraints, and locomotion control could constitute a notable systems contribution. Nevertheless, most individual components are established: PPO locomotion, CNN depth tokenization, state-space sequence models, top-k token pruning, confidence calibration, domain randomization, differentiable planning, and safety fallback controllers. The proposal does not clearly distinguish its gating mechanism from existing dynamic token pruning or selective-computation methods, nor does it provide a sufficiently specific review of prior MAMBA-based robotics, visual control, or multimodal fusion work. Thus, the contribution appears to be an innovative integration rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.

Soundness.justification: The proposal contains several sound practices, including compute-matched baselines, corruption tests, multiple seeds, confidence calibration, effect-size reporting, ablations, hardware benchmarks, and explicit failure-mode analysis. However, key technical claims are not yet rigorously supported. MAMBA's linear sequence processing does not by itself establish long-horizon locomotion foresight, especially because the proposal describes spatial tokens from a depth frame but no explicit temporal sequence or memory protocol. Deterministic top-k selection can remove tokens while disrupting spatial order and terrain coverage, and the proposal does not define positional encoding, ordering, token restoration, or diversity constraints. Computing gates for all tokens and encoding the full image also limits the actual savings, so near-linear scaling does not necessarily imply lower latency than compact CNN or recurrent baselines. The planner and contact model are under-specified, and it is unclear why their auxiliary gradients should improve rather than bias policy features. Hard safety action replacement can create a mismatch between sampled and executed actions, invalidating ordinary PPO likelihood ratios or advantage estimates unless shielded transitions are modeled or excluded carefully. The experimental design also lacks an explicit reward equation, control protocol, sample-unit definition for statistical tests, and a baseline isolating MAMBA from all additional mechanisms. These issues do not make the approach invalid, but they materially weaken its current rigor.

Feasibility.justification: The main building blocks can be implemented with current simulators, reinforcement-learning libraries, MAMBA implementations, differentiable optimization tools, and Orin-class hardware. The staged pilots, deployment microbenchmarks, reduced-budget mode, and explicit latency criteria improve practicality. On the other hand, the complete system is unusually complex: it combines PPO, a selective MAMBA backbone, relaxed top-k routing, confidence calibration, differentiable MPC/iLQR, contact-model learning, domain randomization, a curriculum, system identification, shielding, and real-robot fallback control. Debugging interactions among these components will be difficult. The experiment budget is also very large. Forty million environment steps across 16 seeds for numerous ablations and 30 seeds for final comparisons can require billions of simulated steps, and a full factorial sweep over patch size, token dimension, layer count, gating, planner gradients, and shielding would be prohibitively expensive. Meeting sub-20-millisecond latency on Xavier while running perception, MAMBA, planning, policy inference, confidence estimation, and safety checks is plausible only with careful optimization and may not hold under realistic sensor and system load. The real-world data and safety procedures are too briefly specified for confident deployment.

Significance.justification: Efficient and robust vision-based quadrupedal locomotion is an important robotics problem, and improving robustness under occlusion, depth corruption, latency, and constrained onboard computation would have meaningful practical value. A successful demonstration that selective SSM fusion improves falls, energy use, and deployment latency under matched compute could influence multimodal control architecture design. The proposed confidence and fallback mechanisms may also improve operational reliability. The likely impact is moderated by the fact that the current claims are primarily empirical and depend on a complex collection of components. It is not yet clear whether MAMBA offers a decisive advantage over strong compact CNN-RNN, temporal convolution, recurrent state-space, or efficient-attention baselines. The evaluation terrains are useful but relatively limited, and the real-world protocol is insufficiently developed to support claims of broad sim-to-real robustness.

strengths: Strong alignment with the central vision of compute-aware MAMBA fusion for proprioceptive and depth-based quadrupedal control.
Detailed empirical plan covering corruptions, ablations, confidence calibration, statistical reporting, hardware latency, memory, energy, and safety-related outcomes.
Addresses an important practical problem and explicitly recognizes deployment and sim-to-real risks.
weaknesses: Core architectural details are missing, especially temporal modeling, token ordering, positional treatment after top-k selection, the reward formulation, and the planner-policy interface.
The hard safety shield can violate standard PPO assumptions unless executed actions and shielded transitions are handled explicitly.
The system combines too many auxiliary mechanisms to attribute gains cleanly, while several claimed benefits of MAMBA and token gating are not theoretically or empirically justified.
The proposed seed count and ablation space imply a very large computational budget, and the real-robot validation and safety protocol remain under-specified.
